C0.quote: identify a strongly supported proposal from a space of alternatives
C0.note: Borderline. A deliberation and coalition-formation process aggregates agents' approvals of proposals into a collective choice of the most-supported proposal, framed as pre-vote deliberation.

C1.quote: the deliberation process is guaranteed to terminate
C1.note: Termination bounds (at most n^2 or n^n transitions) are running-time-type results (AL). Most main results are success guarantees for non-strategic coalition-formation dynamics in metric spaces, which fit no listed type (OT).

C2.1.value: approval set; proposals agents approve/support; deliberative coalition structure
C2.1.quote: the set X v is the approval set of v

C2.2.quote: when x >v r we say that v approves x
C2.2.note: Approvals are derived from agents' locations in a metric space: v approves x iff x is closer to v than the status quo.

C2.3.quote: an agent v is able to articulate whether she (strictly) prefers
C2.3.note: Preferences over the status quo and agent locations (ideal points) in a metric space.

C2.4.quote: agents are not strategic: they truthfully reveal whether they support
C2.4.note: Approval is defined as preferring x to the status quo. The conclusion explicitly states truthful revelation; abstracting from strategic issues is stated without justification.

C3.1.quote: in our current model agents are not strategic

C3.2.quote: they truthfully reveal whether they support a given proposal

C3.3.quote: strategic issues that may arise during communication
C3.3.note: The paper says it abstracts away from strategic issues and flags game-theoretic extension as future work; no justification is given.

C4.1.note: No utility, welfare, satisfaction, cost or distortion notions are used for voters; only distances determine approval.

C4.2.note: The term dichotomous preferences is not used.

C5.1.quote: the set of most-supported alternatives is M ∗ = argmaxx∈X\{r} |V x |
C5.1.note: Success is defined by maximum approval support. This is not framed as welfare, efficiency, satisfaction, representation or distortion.

VOT.quote_behav: in our current model agents are not strategic
VOT.note: Agents move between coalitions via permitted transitions, motivated by myopic coalition-size goals. The paper explicitly says agents are not strategic, and the results cover all maximal runs.

OTH.note: An external mediator is mentioned informally but not modelled.

C8.1.note: NA: no type is STRAT or MIXED.

claims.quote: provides formal foundations for the design and development of practical systems
complex deliberative spaces require more sophisticated coalition formation abilities
a foundation for the study of mechanisms and systems allowing communities

C9.2.quote: they truthfully reveal whether they support a given proposal
C9.2.note: Needed assumptions are that approvals reflect preferences over the status quo, agents are non-strategic, and agents follow the specified transitions; all are stated.

C1.reason: The termination bounds justify including AL, but the success guarantees (Theorems 1-3, Propositions 5-8) are the larger share of main results and are best coded OT, so OT is primary.

C2.4.reason: The paper explicitly states that agents truthfully reveal their support, which rules out IDU, and it gives no justification, so IDS applies.

C5.1.reason: Maximum support is a popularity criterion that the paper never frames as welfare, representation or any other listed criterion.

C6.VOT.reason: The paper explicitly declares agents non-strategic, and its results quantify over all permitted runs rather than optimising behaviour; B's own note concedes NONSTRAT is the better reading.

C8.1.reason: With voters coded NONSTRAT and no other type present, C8 does not apply.

C8.2.reason: C8.2 is NA because C8.1 is NA.

C9.2.reason: The needed assumptions (truthful support, non-strategic agents, the transition rules) are all stated, and B's metric-to-real-preference concern is a general modelling-approximation assumption that the codebook excludes.
